description: One day of the European grid's frequency, every second (Energy-Charts, Fraunhofer ISE, measured in Freiburg, Germany). Control idea: in an AC grid the frequency is the balance meter. Every generator spins in step, so a surplus of power speeds them all up and a deficit slows them down; primary control (FCR) then acts like a proportional controller, 3000 MW across Continental Europe in proportion to the deviation, fully used at ±200 mHz, and leaves a small steady error that slower secondary control removes. The steps: seconds → deviation, df/dt and implied FCR power (Polars); minutes for the day chart; the day folded at the quarter-hour; and a paired test, quarter-hour by quarter-hour, of whether the frequency jumps when a quarter-hour turns. The aha: folded at 15 minutes the noise averages out and a sawtooth appears, steepest at the full hour: electricity is traded and scheduled in 15-minute blocks, power plants step their output at the boundaries while demand changes smoothly, and the mismatch is visible as frequency. Caveats: one day and one measuring point (the synchronous area shares one frequency, but local measurements differ by a few mHz in fast events); the FCR power is implied from the standard droop, not measured, and FCR has a ±10 mHz insensitivity; how fast the frequency moves for a given imbalance depends on the grid's inertia (rotating mass), which this data doesn't hold. Change start and end in the query for another day.
name: Grid frequency: the power balance meter
